suggestions.issue: <section> #1 has no <title> — recommended for DITA compliance
context_lines: Abstract: This section covers the Table style in DOCX — the primary structure for presenting information with inherent row-and-column relationships — and ten scenarios: a standard multi-column table, a table with a caption, a table with no header row, merged cells, nested tables, lists and images inside table cells, tables spanning multiple pages, consecutive tables, and a two-column parameter table in a reference topic. The converter reads each table's structure, cell complexity, and topic context to determine whether to map it to <simpletable>, a CALS <table>, or <properties>.

ATable is the primary structure for reference and lookup content. It is a structural mechanism to present information that has inherent row-and-column relationships — parameter names and their values, feature names and their states, error codes and their meanings, API fields and their data types.

A table reduces a lookup task from reading a paragraph to scanning a row and column. In DITA-XML, a table is structured data — each cell is a discrete, addressable unit that a transform can reformat for PDF, or online help output, filter by column for conditional publishing, and extract independently for reuse in other deliverables.

In a .docx file, a table is inserted through Insert → Table and can include a header row, merged cells, and a Caption-styled paragraph. A parameter table typically has a header row and no merged cells. A table with merged cells usually spans a label across several rows and/or columns.

context_lines: Abstract: This section covers document properties and field codes in DOCX — the metadata fields that identify, attribute, and classify a document independently of its body content — and one scenario: document properties populated in the file's properties panel and mapped during conversion. The converter reads each populated property and maps it to the corresponding DITA <prolog> element, making the document's authorship, dates, and classification data available to downstream publishing and search tools.

Metadata is structured information about a document, separate from its body content. It records attributes such as authorship, creation and revision dates, and classification tags. This information is what allows downstream publishing systems, content management platforms, and search indexes to reliably identify, track, and retrieve the document.

In a .docx file, this information lives in two places: document properties, set once for the entire file through File → Info → Properties, and field codes, which display those property values as visible text in the body or cover page (inserted via Insert → Quick Parts → Field Codes). A field code always shows the same value as its source property, even if referenced in multiple places like the header, footer, or cover page.

suggestions.issue: <section> #1 has no <title> — recommended for DITA compliance
context_lines: The metR DOCX to DITA converter does not rely on visual formatting alone. It reads structural information from named Word styles and constructs. When those constructs are applied correctly, the converter and AI Agent can:
• Propose a DITA map hierarchy based on heading levels and topic relationships.
• Detect topic boundaries from heading patterns and semantic signals.
• Classify topic types: concept (descriptive), task (procedural), reference (tabular or lookup), or troubleshooting, and generic.
• Detect reuse candidates such as repeated phrases, shared definitions, and procedural steps.
